L000128	\begin{abstract} \fontsize{13pt}{15pt} \selectfont \bfseries \boldmath
L000129	Many exoplanets have been observed with radius sizes between that of Earth and that of Neptune and are thus classified into two groups: super-earths (SEs) and mini-neptunes (MNs).
L000130	There are no SEs and MNs in the Solar System, and the mechanisms responsible for their formation and evolution are debated.
L000131	We investigate the relationships between the orbital period and eccentricity of SEs and MNs using both ensemble analyses and individual measurements.
L000132	We found that MNs follow an anti-correlation between orbital period and eccentricity, but SEs follow a different relation, possibly in the opposite direction.
L000133	These trends imply that MNs and SEs are dynamically distinct populations.
L000134	We suggest that SEs have been more strongly influenced by violent processes such as gravitational scattering and giant impacts, whereas MNs predominantly experienced quiescent secular evolution.
L000135	\end{abstract}
L000136	
L000137	\clearpage
L000138	\begin{multicols}{2}
L000139	
L000140	
L000141	\noindent The eccentricity of a celestial body's orbit can quantify its dynamic state.
L000142	For a planet or exoplanet, the eccentricity affects the amount of radiation it receives from its host star and therefore its climate and habitability\cite{2002IJAsB...1...61W,2010ApJ...721.1295D,2016A&A...591A.106B}.
L000143	For a population of exoplanets, the distribution of orbital eccentricity and its dependence on other parameters are determined by the formation and evolution mechanisms\cite{2013ApJ...767L..24D,2015PNAS..112...20L,2023PNAS..12017398S}.
L000144	For giant exoplanets, the relationship between orbital period ($P$) and eccentricity ($e$) has been used to investigate their evolution\cite{2005A&A...431.1129H,2018ARA&A..56..175D}, including star-planet tidal interactions\cite{2008ApJ...678.1396J}, planet-planet interactions\cite{2008ApJ...686..621F,2008ApJ...686..580C}, and interactions between planets and the protoplanetary disks from which they formed\cite{2003ApJ...585.1024G,2013ApJ...769...26C}.
L000145	
L000146	For smaller exoplanets, the relationship(s) between $P$ and $e$ is less clear.
L000147	Previous studies have reported a flat $P$--$e$ distribution\cite{2020A&A...635A..37C,2024AJ....168..115B}, unlike the positive correlation found for giant exoplanets\cite{2005A&A...431.1129H,2024AJ....168..115B}.
L000148	Those studies assumed that all exoplanets smaller than a gas giant form a single population, but observations have shown that those exoplanets have a bimodal radius distribution, interpreted as rocky super-earths (SEs) and gaseous mini-neptunes (MNs) separated by a radius valley\cite{2017AJ....154..109F}.
L000149	These are known to be physically distinct classes of exoplanet with different compositions, as indicated by their different densities\cite{2019PNAS..116.9723Z,2022Sci...377.1211L}.
L000150	We therefore investigated the $P$--$e$ relations of MNs and SEs as separate populations.
L000151	
L000152	\subsubsection*{Statistical analysis of transiting exoplanets}
L000153	\noindent We investigated the $P$--$e$ relation of small exoplanets (i.e., those smaller than four Earth radii) orbiting main-sequence stars of spectral types F, G, and K\cite{methods}.
L000154	We adopt a catalogue of transiting exoplanets observed using the Kepler space telescope\cite{methods,2018ApJS..235...38T,KDR25} and then split this sample into SEs and MNs (Fig.~\ref{f1}A) using the empirical position of the radius valley (see Eq.~\ref{es8}).
L000155	
L000156	We statistically inferred the eccentricity distributions of these transiting exoplanets from their distributions of transit duration ratio (TDR)\cite{2008ApJ...678.1407F} as follows:
L000157	\begin{equation}
L000158	{\rm TDR} = \frac{T}{T_0} \sim \frac{\sqrt{(1 - b^2)(1 - e^2)}}{1 - e {\rm sin} \omega},
L000159	\label{eq1}
L000160	\end{equation}
L000161	where $T$ is the observed transit duration, $T_0$ is the expected transit duration for an exoplanet on an equivalent circular orbit (with the observed orbital period) transiting centrally across the stellar disk, $\omega$ is the argument of periapsis of the exoplanet's orbit (i.e., the angle from the orbit's ascending node to periapsis measured in the direction of the exoplanet's motion), and $b$ is the impact parameter of the transit.
L000162	For an individual exoplanet, there are three unknown parameters in this equation, $e$, $\omega$ and $b$, so the eccentricity cannot be uniquely determined.
L000163	However, for a sufficiently large population, the distributions of $\omega$ and $b$ can be inferred from models\cite{2016PNAS..11311431X}, leaving only a single unknown: the eccentricity distribution.
L000164	Therefore, the TDR distribution of a planetary population can be used to statistically reconstruct that population's underlying eccentricity distribution.
L000165	For a statistical population of transiting exoplanets, the values of $b$ approximately follows a uniform distribution between 0 and 1\cite{2016MNRAS.463.1323K}.
L000166	A population of transiting exoplanets on orbits with low eccentricities would thus have a TDR distribution concentrated close to TDR=1 (i.e., the limit of Eq.~\ref{eq1} as $e \to 0$), whereas those on orbits with higher eccentricities would have a more spread-out TDR distribution.
L000167	
L000168	We applied this method to our fiducial sample of SEs and MNs by determining the TDR--$P$ distributions of each population.
L000169	We find that MNs with shorter orbital periods tended to have more spread out TDR values, whereas SEs showed the opposite trend (Fig.~\ref{fs1}).
L000170	
L000171	We divided the SEs and MNs into nine orbital period bins and calculated the mean eccentricities of exoplanets in each using the TDR method\cite{2016PNAS..11311431X,2023AJ....165..125A,methods}.
L000172	For MNs (Fig.~\ref{f1}B), we find that $e$ decreases as $P$ increases, except for the first bin (with $P<4$~days).
L000173	We attribute this discrepant bin to a combination of its high uncertainty and a tidal damping effect.
L000174	The tidal forces between a star and a planet gradually dampen the planet's orbital eccentricity, a process known as tidal circularization.
L000175	The tidal circularization timescales of MNs at $P\approx4$~days are $<1$ billion years (much shorter than the typical age of host stars in our sample), which would produce a peak in the $P$--$e$ diagram (see Supplementary Text).
L000176	For SEs (Fig.~\ref{f1}C), we found that $e$ increase as a function of $P$.
L000177	 \end{multicols}

L000181	\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth]{Figure/Fig.1.png}
L000182	\caption{
L000183	\textbf{Radii and eccentricities of the fiducial Kepler sample.}
L000184	{\bf (A)} Planet radius (in earth radii, $R_\oplus$) as a function of orbital period for SEs (orange squares) and MNs (blue circles) in the fiducial sample of Kepler transits.
L000185	The gray contours show the number density, which was smoothed using Gaussian kernel density estimation.
L000186	The black dashed line indicates the empirical position of the radius valley (see Eq.~\ref{es8}) for an illustrative host star of one solar mass.
L000187	Classification of each exoplanet used the actual observed mass of its host star\cite{methods}.
L000188	{\bf (B)} Mean orbital periods and eccentricities of MNs derived using the TDR method for each orbital period bin.
L000189	{\bf (C)} Same as panel (B), but for SEs.
L000190	All error bars indicate $1~\sigma$ uncertainties
L000191	}
L000192	\label{f1}
L000193	\end{figure}
L000194	
L000195	\begin{multicols}{2}
L000196	\subsubsection*{Comparison with directly measured eccentricities}
L000197	\noindent As a consistency check, we compiled a sample of transiting small exoplanets with precise eccentricity measurements reported in the NASA Exoplanet Archive (NEA) database\cite{2013PASP..125..989A,NEA2024}.
L000198	Unlike the fiducial Kepler sample, the NEA sample consists of exoplanets with individual eccentricity measurements reported by previous studies.
L000199	After application of our selection criteria\cite{methods}, there were 69 exoplanets in this comparison sample.
L000200	We split them into MNs and SEs using the same empirical radius valley (Fig.~\ref{f2}A).
L000201	
L000202	MNs in the comparison sample follow a similar $P$--$e$ trend (Fig.~\ref{f2}B) as in the fiducial sample, with eccentricity generally decreasing with orbital period except for $P\lesssim4$~days.
L000203	For SEs, the comparison sample contains only 11 exoplanets, all with $P\lesssim11$~days and low eccentricities ($e\lesssim0.1$).
L000204	The resulting $P$--$e$ relation (Fig.~\ref{f2}C) is consistent with that of SEs in the fiducial sample (Fig.~\ref{f1}C), but the data are too limited to draw further conclusions.
L000205	We therefore exclude SEs in the comparison sample from our subsequent analyses.
L000206	\end{multicols}
L000207	
L000208	\begin{figure}[!ht]
L000209	\centering
L000210	\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth]{Figure/Fig.2.png}
L000211	\caption{
L000212	\textbf{Radii and eccentricities of the comparison NEA sample.}
L000213	({\bf A} to {\bf C}) Same as Fig.~\ref{f1} but for the comparison sample of individual eccentricity measurements reported in the NEA database\cite{NEA2024}.
L000214	All data points are individual measurements and have not been binned.
L000215	Error bars indicate the $1~\sigma$ uncertainties from previous studies as reported in the NEA database.
L000216	}
L000217	\label{f2}
L000218	\end{figure}
L000219	
L000220	\begin{multicols}{2}
L000221	\subsubsection*{Two distinct \emph{P--e} relations}
L000222	\noindent To quantify the $P$--$e$ relations of MNs and SEs, we fitted the $P$--$e$ distributions with a power-law model: $e = k\cdot(P/(10~{\rm days)})^c$, where $k$ (the amplitude) and $c$ (the power index) are the fitting parameters.
L000223	For the fiducial sample, we re-sampled the mean eccentricity of each orbital period bin by drawing $10^5$ trials from the posterior probability distribution output by the TDR analysis (Fig.~\ref{fs2}).
L000224	In each trial, we fitted the re-sampled $\bar{P}$--$\bar{e}$ distributions (where the bar symbols indicate the mean value in each bin) to obtain values for $k$ and $c$.
L000225	From the $10^5$ re-sampling processes, we fitted $k$ and $c$ $10^5$ times.
L000226	We report their resulting median values, with uncertainties corresponding to the 68.3\% confidence intervals.
L000227	To mitigate the effects of tidal damping, we excluded MNs with $P<4$~days (see the Supplementary Text).
L000228	The results were as follows:
L000229	\end{multicols}
L000230	
L000231	\begin{equation}
L000232	\bar{e} =
L000233	\begin{cases}
L000234	0.165^{+0.019}_{-0.017}\cdot\left(\frac{\bar{P}}{10\;{\rm days}}\right)^{-0.45^{+0.13}_{-0.15}} {\rm ~for~MNs~} (R>R_{\rm valley}) \\
L000235	0.094^{+0.018}_{-0.018}\cdot\left(\frac{\bar{P}}{10\;{\rm days}}\right)^{0.37^{+0.34}_{-0.20}} {\rm ~~~for~SEs~} (R<R_{\rm valley})
L000236	\end{cases}
L000237	,
L000238	\end{equation}
L000239	\begin{multicols}{2}
L000240	\noindent where $R$ and $R_{\rm  valley}$ are, respectively, the planet radius and the position of the radius valley (Eq.~\ref{es8}).
L000241	We apply a similar re-sampling and fitting analysis to MNs from the comparison sample\cite{methods} using the uncertainties on the individual eccentricity measurements reported in the NEA database\cite{NEA2024}.
L000242	The results of fitting comparison sample are shown in Fig.~\ref{f3}B.
L000243	
L000244	Fig.~\ref{f3} compares the best-fitting power-law models with the data.
L000245	MNs in the fiducial sample (Fig.~\ref{f3}A) and comparison samples (Fig.~\ref{f3}B) followed a similar $P$--$e$ anti-correlation.
L000246	SEs follow an opposite trend (Fig.~\ref{f3}C).
L000247	The posterior probability distributions of the power-law indices for MNs and SEs (Fig.~\ref{f3}D) are separated, with minimal overlap.
L000248	The fraction of $c \geq 0$ for MNs is $9.6 \times 10^{-4}$ for the fiducial sample and $7.9 \times 10^{-3}$ for the comparison sample, corresponding to a $P$--$e$ anti-correlation ($c < 0$) at significance levels of $\sim3.3~\sigma$ and $\sim2.7~\sigma$, respectively.
L000249	
L000250	For the SEs in the fiducial sample, the fraction of $c \geq 0$ was 0.982, which indicates a $P$--$e$ positive correlation ($c > 0$) at a significance level of $\sim2.4~\sigma$.
L000251	Although this is only weak evidence of a positive correlation, the difference between SEs and MNs was more significant.
L000252	The posterior probability distributions of $c$ for SEs and MNs in the fiducial sample (Fig.~\ref{f3}D) overlapped by a fraction of $1.9 \times 10^{-4}$, corresponding to a significance level of $\sim 3.7~\sigma$.
L000253	We therefore conclude that SEs and MNs follow different $P$--$e$ relations.
L000254	
L000255	To verify this conclusion, we investigated the effects on the derived $P$--$e$ relations from data binning\cite{methods}, discarding some data points and changing the position of the radius valley, our selection criteria for orbital period and signal-to-noise ratio, observational bias caused by the heterogeneity of the comparison sample, and the use of single-transit exoplanet systems in the fiducial sample (see the Supplementary Text).
L000256	We found that none of these effects change our conclusions.
L000257	
L000258	Previous studies of the $P$--$e$ distributions of small exoplanets\cite{2015ApJ...808..126V,2019AJ....157...61V,2020A&A...635A..37C,2024AJ....168..115B} did not report these relations.
L000259	We attribute this difference from our results to two main causes: previous work (i) studied systems with less precise individual eccentricity measurements (Fig.~\ref{fs21}) and (ii) did not separate SEs from MNs (see the Supplementary Text).
L000260	
L000261	\subsubsection*{Comparison with theoretical models}
L000262	{\noindent \bf SEs}\\
L000263	Dynamical processes that occur during close encounters between planets are known as planet-planet scattering (PPS).
L000264	Theoretical models of PPS have predicted positive correlations between eccentricity and orbital period, as well as between eccentricity and planet mass\cite{2008ApJ...686..621F,2008ApJ...686..580C,2025ApJ...991L..49K}.
L000265	
L000266	A simple model of PPS predicts a $P$--$e$ correlation with $c=1/3$ for a population of equal-mass planets (see the Supplementary Text).
L000267	However, most small planets are observed in systems that have more massive outer planets\cite{2013ApJ...763...41C,2022MNRAS.514.3844C}.
L000268	We therefore expect $c>1/3$ for more realistic populations affected by PPS.
L000269	We adopted a minimum-mass extrasolar nebula (MMEN) model for small planets, which predicts that planetary mass increases with orbital period\cite{2020AJ....159..247D}.
L000270	Combining the MMEN model with the PPS theory, we derive a positive $P$--$e$ correlation with $c\approx0.42$ (see the Supplementary Text).
L000271	Fig.~\ref{f3}C shows this PPS prediction is consistent with the fiducial sample of SEs.
L000272	\end{multicols}
L000273	
L000274	\begin{figure}[!ht]
L000275	\centering
L000276	\includegraphics[width=1\textwidth]{Figure/Fig.3.png}
L000277	\caption{
L000278	\textbf{Comparison of the period--eccentricity relations to theoretical models.}
L000279	{\bf (A)} Filled circles are mean eccentricities (with error bars indicating $1~\sigma$ uncertainties) and mean orbital periods for each orbital period bin in the fiducial Kepler sample.
L000280	The dark blue line is the best-fitting power-law model $e = k\cdot(P/{\rm 10~days})^c$, which has the parameters listed in the legend.
L000281	Light blue lines are 1000 equivalent models randomly drawn from the $10^5$ re-sampling processes.

L000294	\begin{multicols}{2}
L000295	Exoplanets with short orbital periods are expected to experience substantial tidal damping, which lowers their eccentricities.
L000296	This effect is also consistent with our measurement showing that the SEs on short orbital periods ($P \lesssim 6$~days) all exhibit low eccentricities ($\bar{e} \lesssim 0.1$) (Fig.~\ref{f1}C).
L000297	This could indicate that tidal damping also plays a role in establishing the $P$--$e$ positive correlation of SEs  (see the Supplementary Text).
L000298	We were unable to distinguish between these two possibilities, so we conclude that the observed $P$--$e$ distribution of SEs is consistent with the predictions of PPS, tidal damping, or both mechanisms acting simultaneously.
L000299	
L000300	{\noindent \bf MNs}\\
L000301	Long-term (secular) gravitational interactions between multiple planets in the same system are predicted to redistribute angular momentum.
L000302	This effect is expected to dominate in multi-planet systems with well-spaced orbits\cite{2011ApJ...735..109W,2017A&A...605A..72L}.
L000303	Theoretical models quantify this effect using the angular momentum deficit (AMD), the difference in the normal component of the angular momentum between the planet's orbit and a reference orbit (a coplanar circular orbit with the same semi-major axis)\cite{1997A&A...317L..75L,2017A&A...605A..72L}.
L000304	The total AMD in a planetary system is conserved, with any AMD exchange between planets acting towards equipartition\cite{2011ApJ...735..109W}.
L000305	Planets in a system that has reached AMD equipartition all have a similar amount of AMD, which requires their eccentricity to be anti-correlated with both the orbital period and planet mass\cite{2011ApJ...735..109W,2016ApJ...832...34M,2017A&A...605A..72L}.
L000306	For a population of equal-mass planets, full AMD equipartition would produce a $P$--$e$ anti-correlation with $c=-1/6$ (see the Supplementary Text).
L000307	As above, we expect a more realistic distribution of planet masses to produce $c<-1/6$.
L000308	By combining the observed period--mass relation with AMD equipartition theory, we derive a $P$--$e$ anti-correlation with $c\approx-0.31$ (see the Supplementary Text).
L000309	In Fig.~\ref{f3}, panel (A) and (B) show that this expectation is consistent with both samples of MNs.
L000310	
L000311	The $P$--$e$ relation of MNs could also be affected by the host star’s metallicity (i.e., abundance of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium in a star).
L000312	Small planets with shorter orbital periods are observed to preferentially orbit stars with higher metallicity\cite{2016AJ....152..187M}, and small planets around high metallicity stars tend to have higher orbital eccentricities\cite{2023AJ....165..125A}.
L000313	We expect the combination of these two effects to cause some level of $P$--$e$ anti-correlation.
L000314	Using stellar metallicities measured by LAMOST (Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope)\cite{2012RAA....12.1197C} and a Kepler-LAMOST small single-transit planet sample from previous work\cite{2023AJ....165..125A}, we perform a correction for the expected metallicity effect (see the Supplementary Text).
L000315	We found that the $P$--$e$ anti-correlation persisted, with a corrected $c=-0.39^{+0.14}_{-0.15}$ for MNs.
L000316	This value is closer to the prediction for AMD equipartition than the uncorrected measurement.
L000317	
L000318	We also expect MNs with shorter orbital periods and higher eccentricities to be more strongly affected by tidal damping.
L000319	This would decrease the orbital eccentricities of MNs with short orbital periods (see the Supplementary Text), as we observed for $P\lesssim4$~days (Figs.~\ref{f1}B \& \ref{f2}B).
L000320	We therefore conclude that the observed $P$--$e$ distribution of MNs is consistent with the predictions of AMD equipartition, modified by tidal damping at short orbital periods.
L000321	
L000322	\subsubsection*{Implications for exoplanet formation and evolution}
L000323	\noindent The consistency between our results for SEs and the predictions of PPS theory implies that violent processes such as giant impacts, collisions, and fragmentation dominate the orbital evolution of SEs.
L000324	These processes are known to influence planetary system architecture (i.e., the number of planets, their orbital eccentricities, and their orbital inclinations) and planet compositions\cite{2016ApJ...822...54D,2017AJ....154...27M}.
L000325	Compared with MNs, we expect collisions between SEs to produce more surviving large fragments because of their lower escape velocities and generally shorter orbital periods.
L000326	Observations have shown that giant impacts persist in at least some mature systems ($\gtrsim 1$ billion years old), although such events are rare at late epochs \cite{2015ApJ...805...77M}.
L000327	During these dynamic events, SEs could experience substantial atmospheric erosion, losing a large proportion of their volatile envelopes (such as a hydrogen and helium or steam atmosphere).
L000328	This erosion could drive SEs towards compositions similar to rocky planets with thin or absent atmospheres\cite{2015ApJ...812..164L,2015Icar..247...81S,2024ApJ...967...38Z}.
L000329	
L000330	For MNs, the observed $P$--$e$ anti-correlation is consistent with the predictions of AMD equipartition theory, which implies that the evolution of MNs is dominated by secular interactions.
L000331	We expect secular interactions to dominate only in dynamically quiet systems, with minimal influence from PPS and other violent processes.
L000332	Therefore, MNs might have retained the majority of their volatile envelopes, leading to a lower bulk density than SEs.
L000333	For any MNs residing in a more chaotic environment, where PPS and giant impacts dominated their evolution, their resulting dynamical state and $P$--$e$ relation would be primarily influenced by PPS.
L000334	Such exoplanets could experience removal of their volatile envelopes and transition towards a more SE-like composition\cite{2015ApJ...812..164L,2015Icar..247...81S,2024ApJ...967...38Z}.
L000335	
L000336	Although the $P$--$e$ relation of SEs is not consistent with AMD equipartition, this does not preclude the presence of secular interactions in SE systems; it only indicates that they have not reached equilibrium.
L000337	We expect SEs to experience stronger tidal damping and greater influence from PPS than MNs.
L000338	Tidal damping preferentially circularizes short-period orbits, whereas PPS increases eccentricities at longer periods.
L000339	This combination could produce a positive $P$--$e$ correlation for SEs.
L000340	
L000341	In summary, we found that SEs and MNs exhibit different $P$--$e$ relations.
L000342	This indicates that the two populations are in different dynamical states and thus might have experienced different dynamical evolutionary histories.
L000343	We suggest that SEs are more likely to have been affected by (or produced from MNs during) violent events, such as PPS and giant impacts.
L000344	By contrast, the orbits of surviving MNs might have been shaped by secular interactions driving them toward the equipartition of AMD.
L000345	\end{multicols}

L000504	\subsubsection*{\hypertarget{s1.1}{The fiducial Kepler sample}}
L000505	\noindent Our fiducial Kepler sample is built from Kepler data release 25 (Kepler DR25)\cite{2018ApJS..235...38T,KDR25}, which includes 8054 Kepler objects of interest (KOIs) in 6923 systems.
L000506	Table~\ref{ts1} provides an overview of the selection cuts we apply, which are described in detail below.
L000507	
L000508	We first exclude all false positives flagged in the koi\_disposition column of Kepler DR25 catalog (criterion 1), then cross-match the remaining KOIs with a stellar parameter catalog\cite{2020AJ....159..280B}(criterion 2).
L000509	We set a maximum threshold of 1.2 on the renormalized unit weight error (RUWE) reported in Gaia data release 2\cite{2016A&A...595A...1G,2018A&A...616A...1G}, chosen to filter out potential binary stars (criterion 3).
L000510	We use Gaia data release 2 for consistency with the stellar parameters catalog\cite{2020AJ....159..280B}.
L000511	We have checked that using Gaia data release 3\cite{2023A&A...674A...1G} has a negligible effect on the results.
L000512	We also set an lower limit of 0.99 on the goodness of fit (GOF) parameter in the stellar parameter catalog to ensure the robustness of stellar parameters.
L000513	We then apply stellar parameter cuts of $\log_{10}(g\cdot{\rm s}^2\cdot{\rm cm}^{-1})>4$ on the surface gravity $g$, to select main sequence stars (criterion 5) and effective temperatures $4700{\rm K} < T_{\rm eff} < 6500{\rm K}$ (criterion 6) to focus on FGK-type stars.
L000514	This ensures that all exoplanets in our sample have similar host stars\cite{2017AJ....154..109F,2018ApJ...866...99B}.
L000515	After applying all the above criteria, we are left with 2651 exoplanets in 1978 systems.

L000568	\subsubsection*{\hypertarget{s1.2}{TDR method}}
L000569	\noindent We estimate the eccentricity distribution of a group of transiting exoplanets from their TDR distribution\cite{2008ApJ...678.1407F}.
L000570	TDR is defined as the ratio of the planetary transit duration $T$ to a reference duration $T_0$ (Eq.~\ref{eq1}), which is the transit duration that an exoplanet would have if its orbit was circular and the transit impact parameter was zero (assuming $m \ll M_{\star}$, where $m$ and $M_{\star}$ are the mass of the exoplanet and the mass of the host star, respectively):
L000571	\begin{equation}
L000572	\label{es1}
L000573	T_0 = \frac{(R+R_\star) P}{\pi a} = \left(\frac{3}{{\rm G}\pi^2}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} \left( \frac{P}{\rho_\star} \right)^{\frac{1}{3}}(1 + r),
L000574	\end{equation}
L000575	where $a$, $\rho_{\star}$ and G are the planetary orbital semi-major axis, the stellar density, and the universal gravitational constant, respectively.
L000576	
L000577	We perform forward modeling to generate simulated TDR (${\rm TDR}_{\rm sim}$) following previous work\cite{2016PNAS..11311431X,2023AJ....165..125A}.
L000578	Then we apply the maximum likelihood estimation approach to fit ${\rm TDR}_{\rm sim}$ to the observed TDR (${\rm TDR}_{\rm obs}$).
L000579	The likelihood function is:
L000580	\end{multicols}
L000581	
L000582	\begin{equation}
L000583	\label{es2}
L000584	\mathcal{L}({\rm TDR}_{\rm obs} | \bar{e}) = \int {\rm PDF}({\rm TDR}_{\rm sim} | \bar{e}) \cdot {\rm exp} \left[ -\frac{({\rm TDR}_{\rm sim} - {\rm TDR}_{\rm obs})^2}{2 \sigma_{{\rm TDR}}^2} \right] {\rm d} {\rm TDR}_{\rm sim},
L000585	\end{equation}
L000586	
L000587	\begin{multicols}{2}
L000588	\noindent where $\bar{e}$ is the mean orbital eccentricity of a group of exoplanets, $\sigma_{\rm TDR}$ is the uncertainty of ${\rm TDR}_{\rm obs}$ and ${\rm PDF}({\rm TDR}_{\rm sim} | \bar{e})$ is the probability density function (PDF) of the simulated TDR (with mean eccentricity of $\bar{e}$).
L000589	By maximizing Eq.~\ref{es2}, we obtain the best fitting value of $\bar{e}$.
L000590	\end{multicols}
L000591	\begin{multicols}{2}
L000592	To estimate ${\rm PDF}({\rm TDR}_{\rm sim} | \bar{e})$ in Eq.~\ref{es2}, we randomly assign $e$, $\omega$ and $I_{\rm p}$ (the planetary inclination relative to the observer) for each exoplanet in our sample to obtain the distribution of ${\rm TDR}_{\rm sim}$.
L000593	Specifically, $e$ is drawn from a Rayleigh distribution, $\omega$ is drawn from a uniform distribution between 0 and $2\pi$, and $I_{\rm p}$ is assigned by assuming ${\rm cos}I_{\rm p}$ follows a uniform distribution between -1 and 1.
L000594	After the assignment, the transit impact parameter $b$ of each exoplanet is calculated via (assuming $m \ll M_{\star}$):
L000595	\end{multicols}
L000596	
L000597	\begin{equation}
L000598	\label{es3}
L000599	b = \frac{a {\rm cos}I_{\rm p}}{R_\star}  \frac{1-e^2}{1-e {\rm sin}\omega} = \left(\frac{{\rm G}}{3\pi}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} P^{\frac{2}{3}} \rho_\star^{\frac{1}{3}} \frac{1-e^2}{1-e {\rm sin}\omega} {\rm cos}I_{\rm p},
L000600	\end{equation}
L000601	
L000602	\begin{multicols}{2}
L000603	\noindent where $\omega$ is the argument of periapsis of the exoplanet's orbit, differing by $\pi$ radians from the argument of periapsis of the star's orbit due to the exoplanet ($\omega_\star = \omega+\pi$).
L000604	The modeled transit duration of each exoplanet is calculated via:
L000605	\begin{equation}
L000606	\label{es4}
L000607	T = \frac{P}{\pi} \frac{(1 - e^2)^\frac{3}{2}}{(1 - e {\rm sin} \omega)^2} {\rm arcsin} \left[ \frac{\sqrt{(1 + r)^2 - b^2}}{b \tan I_{\rm p}} \right],
L000608	\end{equation}
L000609	To simulate an observation, we consider the observational uncertainties of $T_0$ and $T$.
L000610	We obtain the simulated transit duration by assuming it has the same relative uncertainty as the observation:
L000611	\begin{equation}
L000612	\label{es5}
L000613	T_{\rm sim} = T + R_{\rm N1} \sigma_{T_{\rm obs}} \frac{T}{T_{\rm obs}},
L000614	\end{equation}
L000615	where $\sigma_{T_{\rm obs}}$ is the uncertainty of $T_{\rm obs}$ and $R_{\rm N1}$ is a random variable drawn from a normal distribution with median of 0 and standard deviation of 1.
L000616	Similarly, we obtain simulated reference transit duration by assuming it has the same uncertainty as the observation:
L000617	\begin{equation}
L000618	\label{es6}
L000619	T_{0\rm sim} = T_0 + R_{\rm N2} \sigma_{T_0},
L000620	\end{equation}
L000621	where $\sigma_{T_0}$ is the uncertainty of $T_0$ and $R_{\rm N2}$ is a random variable drawn from a normal distribution with median of 0 and standard deviation of 1.
L000622	Following previous work\cite{2014ApJ...790..146F}, we assign a simulated SNR for each $T_{\rm sim}$:
L000623	\begin{equation}
L000624	\label{es7}
L000625	{\rm SNR}_{\rm sim} = {\rm SNR}_{\rm obs} \sqrt{\frac{T_{\rm sim}}{T_{\rm obs}}},
L000626	\end{equation}
L000627	where ${\rm SNR}_{\rm sim}$ and ${\rm SNR}_{\rm obs}$ are the simulated SNR and observed SNR, respectively.

L000629	Otherwise, we continue to calculate the simulated TDR (${\rm TDR}_{\rm sim}=T_{\rm sim}/T_{0\rm sim}$).
L000630	These steps are repeated until at least 300 ${\rm TDR}_{\rm sim}$ are assembled for each exoplanet.
L000631	We then calculate the mean eccentricity ($\bar{e}$) of these exoplanets and use the Gaussian kernel density estimation (KDE) to estimate ${\rm PDF}({\rm TDR}_{\rm sim})$.
L000632	We vary the mean value of the Rayleigh distribution to obtain ${\rm PDF}({\rm TDR}_{\rm sim} | \bar{e})$.

L000803	\subsubsection*{\hypertarget{s2.2}{Effect of eccentricity uncertainty cut}}
L000804	\noindent For criteria 4 and 5 in the comparison NEA sample, we adopt $\varepsilon < 0.12$ and $\eta < 120\%$, where $\varepsilon$ is the absolute eccentricity error and $\eta$ is the relative eccentricity error.
L000805	To investigate the effect of these eccentricity uncertainty cuts, we investigate 14 alternative samples by modifying criterion 4 and criterion 5 to $\varepsilon < \varepsilon_{\rm max}$ and $\eta < \eta_{\rm max}$, with $\varepsilon_{\rm max}$ (the upper limit of $\varepsilon$) varying from 0.07 to 0.48 and $\eta_{\rm max}$ (the upper limit of $\eta$) from 70\% to 480\%.
L000806	We define a dimensionless number $u$ to quantify the combined uncertainty, where:
L000807	\begin{equation}
L000808	\label{es9}
L000809	u = 0.5\varepsilon + 0.05\eta.
L000810	\end{equation}
L000811	Among our 15 samples (including the comparison NEA sample with $u_{\rm max}=0.12$), $u_{\rm max}$ (the upper limit of $u$) varies from 0.07 to 0.48.
L000812	Because there are insufficient SEs in these NEA samples, we focus only on MNs in the statistical analysis (see main text).
L000813	We divide MNs in these samples into multiple bins according to their orbital periods to investigate their $P$--$e$ relations.
L000814	We apply orbital period boundaries of (4, 6, 10, 20) days to divide the samples with more than 50 exoplanets (with $u_{\rm max}>0.09$, including our comparison NEA sample) into five bins.
L000815	For samples with less than 50 exoplanets (with $u_{\rm max}\leq0.09$), we apply four bins with boundaries of (4, 8, 20) days.
L000816	These binning criteria ensure that each data bin contains a similar number of plants, while remaining similar to the binning criteria used in our fiducial Kepler sample.
L000817	For the following statistical analysis, similar to our fiducial Kepler sample, we exclude the first bins of these samples to avoid the effect of tidal damping (corresponding to an orbital period cut of $P>4$ days, see Supplementary Text).
L000818	Then we bootstrap $10^5$ times to obtain the distributions of mean orbital period and mean orbital eccentricity in each bin.
L000819	The median values of $\bar{P}$ and $\bar{e}$ are reported for each bin, with uncertainties corresponding to their 68.3\% confidence intervals, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fs8}.
L000820	
L000821	The bootstrap procedure is constructed as follow:
L000822	In each iteration, we first randomly select exoplanets with replacements to form a new sub-sample with the same size as the original bin.
L000823	This is equivalent to randomly assigning a weight to each exoplanet in the data bin.
L000824	Secondly, we re-sample the eccentricities of each exoplanet according to their reported uncertainties (assuming they follow Gaussian distributions).
L000825	To avoid negative eccentricities in data re-sample process, we follow previous work\cite{2017A&A...605A..72L} by using $e{\rm sin}\omega$ and $e{\rm cos}\omega$ (instead of $e$) to build the Gaussian distribution.
L000826	After data re-sampling, we calculate the mean orbital period and mean eccentricity of exoplanets in each bin, and fit a power-law model ($e = k\cdot(P/(10~{\rm days)})^c$) to the mean orbital periods and mean eccentricities.
L000827	The fractions of samples with $c\geq0$ is taken as the p-value of a $P$--$e$ anti-correlation.
L000828	The median and corresponding 68.3\% confidence intervals of the posterior probability distributions of each parameter ($k$ and $c$) from $10^5$ fitting processes are taken as the fitting values and $1~\sigma$ uncertainties.
L000829	The results of fitting 15 samples (with $P>4$ days) are shown in Fig.~\ref{fs8}.
L000830	
L000831	Fig.~\ref{fs9} shows the sizes and fitting parameters as a function of the parameterized uncertainties ($u_{\rm max}$) for 15 samples (with $P>4$ days).
L000832	The sample sizes and fitting parameters vary with the applied uncertainty cuts.
L000833	We find p-value $<0.05$, corresponding to a significance $>2~\sigma$  for a $P$--$e$ anti-correlation appears for $u_{\rm max}\in[0.08,0.18]$.
L000834	As the uncertainties grow, the best-fitting power-law index $c$ gradually approaches zero, and the p-value gradually increases beyond 0.05 (significance drops below $2~\sigma$), indicating significance of the $P$--$e$ anti-correlation of MNs becomes weaker and is eventually overwhelmed by the increasing uncertainty (Fig.~\ref{fs8}J-O).
L000835	In the other direction, as the uncertainty decreases, the sample size (number of exoplanets) becomes too small to obtain reliable fitting results, causing the p-value to increase as well(Fig.~\ref{fs8}A-C).
L000836	However, for sample sizes varying from 27 to 58, the fitting parameter $c$ remains stable (consistent within $1~\sigma$), and the p-value remains $<0.05$ (significance $>2~\sigma$).
L000837	We conclude that the $P$--$e$ relation of MNs is detected for eccentricity precision $u < 0.18$ and sample size $N_{\rm p} \gtrsim 30$.

L000873	\subsection*{\hypertarget{s3}{Theoretical \emph{P--e} relation}}
L000874	\subsubsection*{\hypertarget{s3.1}{Planet-planet scattering}}
L000875	\noindent The orbital eccentricities of planets can be excited via PPS\cite{1996Sci...274..954R,1996Natur.384..619W}.
L000876	The growth of eccentricity through PPS is proportional to the ratio of a planet's surface escape velocity to its orbital velocity\cite{2008ApJ...686..621F,2008ApJ...686..580C}:
L000877	\begin{equation}
L000878	\label{es10}
L000879	e = \beta \frac{v_{\rm esc}}{v_{\rm orb}} = \beta \sqrt{\frac{2ma}{M_\star R}},
L000880	\end{equation}
L000881	where $\beta$ is a coefficient that quantifies the efficiency of eccentricity excitation, $v_{\rm esc}$ is a planet's escape velocity, and $v_{\rm orb}$ is a planet's orbital velocity.
L000882	
L000883	The theory of PPS can be used to estimate the eccentricity induced by close encounters between planets.
L000884	We adopt an $m$--$R$ relation for SEs\cite{2020A&A...634A..43O}:
L000885	\begin{equation}
L000886	\label{es11}
L000887	\frac{m}{M_\oplus} = 0.90\left(\frac{R}{R_\oplus}\right)^{3.45},
L000888	\end{equation}
L000889	where $M_\oplus$ is the mass of Earth, and apply Kepler's Third Law (assuming $m \ll M_{\star}$), Eq.~\ref{es10} can be rewritten as:
L000890	\begin{equation}
L000891	\label{es12}
L000892	e \approx 0.15\beta \left(\frac{M_{\star}}{M_\odot}\right)^{-\frac{1}{3}} \left(\frac{R}{1.3\;R_\oplus}\right)^{1.2} \left({\frac{P}{10\;{\rm days}}}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}.
L000893	\end{equation}
L000894	Eq.~\ref{es12} gives the typical orbital eccentricities of SEs in our fiducial Kepler sample.
L000895	From Eq.~\ref{es12} we find that for planets with similar sizes (around host stars with similar $M_{\star}$), the theory of PPS predicts a positive correlation between orbital period and eccentricity, with a power-law index of $c=1/3$.
L000896	This value is consistent with our measured value for SEs ($c=0.37^{+0.34}_{-0.20}$).
L000897	Fitting Eq.~\ref{es12} to the observed $P$--$e$ distribution of SEs in our fiducial Kepler sample gives $\beta \approx 0.7$ (for $M_{\star}=1~M_\odot$).
L000898	
L000899	However, given that most small exoplanets systems have outer exoplanets more massive than the inner one\cite{2013ApJ...763...41C,2022MNRAS.514.3844C}, we consider the connection between planet mass and orbital period via the MMEN model\cite{2004ApJ...612.1147K,2013MNRAS.431.3444C,2020AJ....159..247D}.
L000900	MMEN is an in-situ formation model designed to represent the formation and evolution of SEs.
L000901	It assumes that the surface density profile $\Sigma(a)$ of solid planet-building materials in the protoplanetary disk is:
L000902	\begin{equation}
L000903	\label{es13}
L000904	\Sigma(a) = a^\alpha \Sigma_0,
L000905	\end{equation}
L000906	where $\Sigma_0$ is a scaling coefficient and $\alpha$ is the power-law index of the solid surface density profile.
L000907	The exoplanet mass predicted by MMEN is:
L000908	\begin{equation}
L000909	\label{es14}
L000910	m = 2\pi a \Delta a \Sigma(a),
L000911	\end{equation}
L000912	where $\Delta a$ spans the accretion zone of an exoplanet.
L000913	Following previous work\cite{1998Icar..131..171K,2020AJ....159..247D}, we adopt $\Delta a=10R_{\rm Hill}$, where $R_{\rm Hill}$ is the Hill radius of an exoplanet:
L000914	\begin{equation}
L000915	\label{es15}
L000916	R_{\rm Hill} =a \left(\frac{m}{3M_\star}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}.
L000917	\end{equation}
L000918	Combining Eq.~\ref{es13}, Eq.~\ref{es14} and Eq.~\ref{es15}, we obtain:
L000919	\begin{equation}
L000920	\label{es16}
L000921	m \approx 288\Sigma_0^{\frac{3}{2}} M_\star^{-\frac{1}{2}} a^{\frac{6+3\alpha}{2}}.
L000922	\end{equation}
L000923	Combining Eq.~\ref{es10}, Eq.~\ref{es11}, Eq.~\ref{es16}, and apply Kepler's Third Law (assuming $m \ll M_{\star}$), we find:
L000924	\begin{equation}
L000925	\label{es17}
L000926	e \approx 0.09\beta \left(\frac{M_{\star}}{M_\odot}\right)^{-0.47} \left({\frac{P}{10\;{\rm days}}}\right)^{0.42},
L000927	\end{equation}
L000928	for $\Sigma_0=50~{\rm g \cdot cm^{-2}}\cdot{\rm au}^{-\alpha}$ and $\alpha=-1.75$\cite{2020AJ....159..247D}, where au is the astronomical units.
L000929	Eq.~\ref{es17} has an exponent of $c\approx0.42$, which is consistent with our measurement for SEs, and more closely matches the $P$--$e$ relation of SEs after correcting the effect of stellar metallicity (see below).
L000930	Fitting Eq.~\ref{es17} to the observed $P$--$e$ distribution of SEs in our fiducial Kepler sample gives $\beta \approx 1$ (for $M_{\star}=1~M_\odot$), indicating efficient eccentricity excitation.
L000931	However, in this model, the value of $\beta$ is dependent on $\Sigma_0$ ($\beta \sim \Sigma_0 ^{-0.53}$).
L000932	For example, if we adopt a larger $\Sigma_0=100~{\rm g \cdot cm^{-2}}\cdot{\rm au}^{-\alpha}$ derived from RV measurements\cite{2020AJ....159..247D}, we find $\beta \approx 0.7$.
L000933	
L000934	\subsubsection*{\hypertarget{s3.2}{Angular momentum deficit equipartition}}
L000935	\noindent In a planetary system that is well spaced, if planets are not in exact resonance, the dynamical evolution is governed by long-range secular interactions among planets.
L000936	In the secular dynamical evolution, the total AMD is conserved while exchanging among different planets\cite{1997A&A...317L..75L,2000PhRvL..84.3240L,2017A&A...605A..72L}, ultimately leading to AMD equipartition among different planets in the planetary systems\cite{1989Icar...77..330W,2011ApJ...735..109W,2017A&A...605A..72L}.
L000937	Planets near mean motion resonances (MMR) are expected to reach AMD equipartition more quickly\cite{2011ApJ...735..109W}.
L000938	
L000939	The AMD is defined as the difference in the normal component of angular momentum (with respect to the system invariant plane) that a planet has compared to what it would have if its orbit was circular and coplanar (assuming $m \ll M_{\star}$)\cite{2017A&A...605A..72L}:
L000940	\begin{equation}
L000941	\label{es18}
L000942	{\rm AMD}= m \sqrt{{\rm G}M_{\star}a}(1-\sqrt{1-{e}^2}{\rm{cos}}i),
L000943	\end{equation}
L000944	where $i$ is the inclination of the planet relative to the system invariant plane.
L000945	
L000946	As the system approaches AMD equipartition, the AMD of each planet in the system becomes nearly equal.
L000947	Assuming both orbital eccentricity and inclination are low ($e^2\sim0$ and $i\sim0$), Eq.~\ref{es18} indicates the eccentricity of a planet is:
L000948	\begin{equation}
L000949	\label{es19}
L000950	e \approx \left(\frac{4{\rm AMD_0}^2}{{\rm G}M_{\star}} \right)^{\frac{1}{4}} m^{-\frac{1}{2}}a^{-\frac{1}{4}},
L000951	\end{equation}
L000952	where $\rm AMD_0$ is the AMD of a planet.
L000953	We rewrite Eq.~\ref{es19} as:
L000954	\begin{equation}
L000955	\label{es20}
L000956	e \approx 1.92{\rm AMD_0}^{\frac{1}{2}}({{\rm G}M_{\star}})^{-\frac{1}{3}}m^{-\frac{1}{2}}P^{-\frac{1}{6}},
L000957	\end{equation}
L000958	by applying Kepler's Third Law (assuming $m \ll M_{\star}$).
L000959	From Eq.~\ref{es20}, we find that for planets with similar masses (around host stars with similar $M_{\star}$), AMD equipartition predicts an anti-correlation between orbital period and eccentricity, with a power-law index $c=-1/6$.
L000960	This is substantially weaker than our measured value for MNs ($c=-0.45^{+0.13}_{-0.15}$).
L000961	Therefore, we further consider the correlation between orbital period and planet mass.
L000962	
L000963	Because the formation and evolution of MNs can involve orbital migration, instead of using the MMEN model, we adopt an empirical $P$--$m$ relation from observations.
L000964	We collect a sample of multi-planet systems (each containing at least one MN with $R_{\rm valley}<R<4~R_\oplus$) with precise mass measurement in the NEA catalog, with these selection criteria:
L000965	\begin{enumerate}
L000966	\item Planetary parameter cut: $0<R<4~R_\oplus$, $0<m<13~M_{\rm J}$, and only include exoplanets that are measured by both transit and RV methods.
L000967	\item Relative mass uncertainty cut: $(m_{\rm upper} +  m_{\rm lower})<m$, where $m_{\rm upper}$ and $m_{\rm lower}$ are the upper and lower mass uncertainties of the exoplanet, respectively.
L000968	\item Stellar parameter cut: $4700~{\rm K} < T_{\rm eff} < 6500~{\rm K}$, $\log_{10}(g\cdot{\rm s}^2\cdot{\rm cm}^{-1})>4$ , and exclude circumbinary exoplanet systems.
L000969	\end{enumerate}
L000970	These cuts result in 52 exoplanets in 22 systems in the sample, and their $P$--$m$ distribution is shown in the left panel of Fig.~\ref{fs10}A.
L000971	
L000972	We fitted the $P$--$m$ distribution of exoplanets in each multi-planet system with a power-law model: $m/M_\oplus=h\cdot(P/(10~{\rm day}))^d$, where $h$ (amplitude) and $d$ (index) are the fitting parameters.
L000973	The distribution of 22 power-law indices $d$ is shown in Fig.~\ref{fs10}B.
L000974	To account for the uncertainties of the mass measurements, we obtain a alternative distribution of $d$ by performing bootstrap  re-sampling.
L000975	Specifically, for each system, we re-sample the planet mass 100 times according to their reported error uncertainties (by assuming they follow Gaussian distributions).
L000976	In each re-sample process, we fitted a power-law model to the $P$--$m$ distribution of exoplanets in each multi-planet system to obtain 100 fitting parameters ($h$ and $d$) for each system.
L000977	The distribution of the resulting 2200 values of $d$ is also shown in Fig.~\ref{fs10}B.
L000978	
L000979	Most of these multi-planet systems follow a positive $P$--$m$ correlation ($d>0$), and the median $P$--$m$ correlation (from the bootstrapping distribution) is:
L000980	\begin{equation}
L000981	\label{es21}
L000982	\frac{m}{M_\oplus} = 8.72\left(\frac{P}{10\;{\rm days}}\right)^{0.29}.
L000983	\end{equation}
L000984	The median power-law index ($d=0.29$) of the observed $P$--$m$ correlation of MNs is similar to that predicted by MMEN model ($d=0.25$, calculated using Eq.~\ref{es16} with $\alpha=-1.75$)\cite{2020AJ....159..247D}.
L000985	Combining Eq.~\ref{es21} with Eq.~\ref{es20}, we obtain:
L000986	\end{multicols}
L000987	
L000988	\begin{equation}
L000989	\label{es22}
L000990	e \approx 0.20 \left(\frac{\rm AMD_0}{\rm AMD_{Neptune}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \left(\frac{M_{\star}}{M_\odot}\right)^{-\frac{1}{3}}  \left({\frac{P}{10\;{\rm days}}}\right)^{-0.31},
L000991	\end{equation}
L000992	
L000993	\begin{multicols}{2}
L000994	\noindent where $\rm AMD_{Neptune}$ is the AMD of Neptune in the Solar system.
L000995	The exponent in Eq.~\ref{es22} is negative, which implies an anti-correlation between orbital period and eccentricity.
L000996	This predicted power-law index of $c\approx-0.31$ is $1.1~\sigma$ larger than our measured value for MNs ($c=-0.45^{+0.13}_{-0.15}$).
L000997	This slight difference could be explained by the effect of stellar metallicity (see below).
L000998	Fitting Eq.~\ref{es22} to the observed $P$--$e$ distribution of MNs in our fiducial Kepler sample gives ${\rm AMD_0}\approx 0.65\rm AMD_{Neptune}$ (for $M_{\star}=1~M_\odot$).
L000999	\end{multicols}

L001019	\subsubsection*{\hypertarget{s3.3}{Effect of tidal damping}}
L001020	\noindent In principle, planets with shorter orbital periods should undergo stronger gravitational tidal interactions, which act to circularize their orbits.
L001021	If we consider only the effect of the gravitational tide raised on the planet by the star, the equilibrium tide can be approximately described by a constant $Q$ model (where $Q$ is tidal quality factor).
L001022	By assuming $e^2\sim0$ and ignoring the stellar tides, we have\cite{1966Icar....5..375G,2008ApJ...678.1396J}:
L001023	\begin{equation}
L001024	\label{es23}
L001025	{\frac{1}{e}} \frac{{\rm d}e}{{\rm d}t}  = -\frac{1}{\tau_e},
L001026	\end{equation}
L001027	where $\tau_e$ is the tidal circularization timescale:
L001028	\begin{equation}
L001029	\label{es24}
L001030	\tau_e = Q'{\frac{P}{21\pi}}\frac{m}{M_{\star}}\left({\frac{a}{R}}\right)^5,
L001031	\end{equation}
L001032	$Q'\equiv Q/k_2$ is the modified tidal quality factor and $k_2$ is the second Love number.
L001033	The smaller the $Q'$, the stronger the tidal damping effect.
L001034	The values of $Q'$ for small exoplanets (SEs and MNs) are highly uncertain  \cite{2017AJ....153...86M,2018AJ....155..157P,2023ApJ...958L..21L}.
L001035	It could range from $\sim 10^2$ (rocky planet)\cite{2016CeMDA.126..145L} to $\sim 10^5$ (Neptunian planet)\cite{2008Icar..193..267Z}.
L001036	It has been predicted that SEs have a smaller $Q'$ ($\sim 10^3$, closer to the rocky value) than MNs ($\sim 10^4$, closer to the Neptunian value)\cite{2023ApJ...958L..21L}.
L001037	
L001038	To evaluate the tidal circularization timescales of SEs and MNs, we adopt $m$--$R$ relations\cite{2020A&A...634A..43O}:
L001039	\begin{equation}
L001040	\label{es25}
L001041	\frac{m}{M_\oplus}  =
L001042	\begin{cases}
L001043	1.74\left(\frac{R}{R_\oplus}\right)^{1.58}~{\rm for~MNs}  ~(R>R_{\rm  valley}) \\
L001044	0.90\left(\frac{R}{R_\oplus}\right)^{3.45}~{\rm for~SEs} ~(R<R_{\rm  valley})
L001045	\end{cases}
L001046	.
L001047	\end{equation}
L001048	Combining Eq.~\ref{es24} with Eq.~\ref{es25}, we obtain:
L001049	\end{multicols}
L001050	
L001051	\begin{equation}
L001052	\label{es26}
L001053	\tau_e =
L001054	\begin{cases}
L001055	4.5~{\rm Gyrs} \; \frac{Q'}{10^4}  \left(\frac{M_\star}{M_\odot}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}  \left({\frac{P}{6\;{\rm days}}}\right)^{\frac{13}{3}} \left({\frac{R}{2.5~R_\oplus}}\right)^{-3.42}, ~{\rm for~MNs}  ~(R>R_{\rm  valley}) \\
L001056	3.6~{\rm Gyrs} \; \frac{Q'}{10^3}  \left(\frac{M_\star}{M_\odot}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}  \left({\frac{P}{6\;{\rm days}}}\right)^{\frac{13}{3}} \left({\frac{R}{1.3~R_\oplus}}\right)^{-1.55}, ~{\rm for~SEs}  ~(R<R_{\rm  valley})
L001057	\end{cases}
L001058	.
L001059	\end{equation}
L001060	
L001061	\begin{multicols}{2}
L001062	\noindent Eq.~\ref{es26} gives the typical tidal circularization timescales of SEs and MNs in the fiducial Kepler sample.
L001063	SEs (MNs) exhibit stronger (weaker) self-gravitation than rocky (Neptunian) planets, which will lead to weaker (stronger) tidal damping.
L001064	Taking into account this size effect\cite{2012ApJ...746..150E}, we consider a larger $Q'$ of SEs compared to rocky planets and a smaller $Q'$ of MNs compared to Neptunian planets in Eq.~\ref{es26}, following previous work\cite{2023ApJ...958L..21L}.
L001065	
L001066	The median stellar ages of SEs and MNs in our fiducial Kepler sample are 4.1 and 4.7 Gyrs, respectively, so we expect exoplanets with short orbital periods ($P\lesssim6$ days) to undergo prominent tidal circularization.
L001067	From Fig.~\ref{f1}B-C, we find that tidal damping is prominent for exoplanets with short orbital periods ($\lesssim$4−6 days), affecting a larger fraction (4 of 9 bins) of SEs than MNs (1 of 9 bins) in our fiducial Kepler sample.
L001068	We infer that the eccentricity distributions of both SEs and MNs in these short-period systems are consistent with the effects of tidal damping.
L001069	
L001070	For MNs, the lower eccentricity of the first bin in Fig.~\ref{f1}B (with $P<4$ days) appears to violate the $P$--$e$ anti-correlation.
L001071	We interpret this as due to effect of tidal damping.
L001072	The eccentricity of the second bin in Fig.~\ref{f1}B (with $4~{\rm days}<P<6~{\rm days}$) appears unaffected by tidal damping, and remains consistent with the overall $P$--$e$ anti-correlation (see below).
L001073	We attribute this to the AMD transfer.
L001074	In the AMD equipartition scenario, AMD can be continuously transferred to the inner exoplanets over a timescale $\tau_{\rm AMD}\sim100$ Myrs\cite{2011ApJ...735..109W}, maintaining their eccentricities.
L001075	According to Eq.~\ref{es26}, the tidal circularization timescales of MNs with $P\in$ (4,6) days are $\sim$ Gyrs, much longer than their AMD equipartition timescales ($\tau_e \gg \tau_{\rm AMD}$).
L001076	This could explain the weaker tidal damping in the second bin, which is consistent with the overall $P$--$e$ anti-correlation.
L001077	Therefore, we conclude that an initial eccentricity distribution anti-correlated with orbital periods is consistent with our observation, while the lower eccentricities in short periods can be explained by the effect of tidal damping.
L001078	
L001079	For SEs, the first four bins (with $P<6$ days) all display low eccentricities: $\bar{e}\lesssim0.1$ (Fig.~\ref{f1}C).
L001080	This indicates that tidal damping plays a role in the positive $P$--$e$ correlation of SEs.
L001081	If SEs initially exhibited eccentricities independent of orbital periods ($e=e_0$), tidal damping would produce a nearly bimodal eccentricity distribution ($e\sim0$ in short orbital period regime, and $e\sim e_0$ in long orbital period regime).
L001082	Instead, we observe a gradually increasing trend in the $P$--$e$ distribution of SEs (Fig.~\ref{f3}C).
L001083	Therefore, we find that an initial eccentricity distribution positively correlated with orbital periods, in line with the predictions of the PPS model, is more consistent with the observed characteristics of SEs.
L001084	However, the $\sim~2.4\sigma$ statistical significance of this correlation is low, particularly when short-period ($P\lesssim6$ days) exoplanets are excluded from the analyses (see below).
L001085	
L001086	Furthermore, the tentatively positive $P$--$e$ correlation does not exclude secular interactions in SE systems, rather it indicates that they have not reached AMD equipartition.
L001087	Secular interactions tend to transfer AMD to inner exoplanets within the systems, thereby increasing their orbital eccentricities.
L001088	However, stronger tidal effects (due to shorter orbital periods and smaller tidal quality factors compared to MNs) simultaneously damp the eccentricities of these inner SEs, causing them to migrate inward (a process that further strengthens the tidal effect).
L001089	This would cause SEs with short orbital periods in mature systems to exhibit low eccentricities.
L001090	A potential evidence of this ongoing excitation-damping process is that observed SEs with short orbital periods show low but non-zero eccentricities\cite{2020A&A...635A..37C,2024AJ....168..115B}.
L001091	Therefore, we propose that the positive $P$--$e$ relation of SEs is consistent with the combined effect of PPS, tidal damping and secular interactions.
L001092	While the moderate eccentricities in long orbital periods (where the effect of tidal damping and secular interactions can be ignored) can be explained by PPS, the lower eccentricities in short periods (where the effect of PPS can be ignored) agree with the joint effect of tidal damping and secular interactions

L001244	\subsubsection*{\hypertarget{s8.1}{TTV systems and MMR systems}}
L001245	\noindent The exoplanets in our comparison NEA samples were detected and characterized using transit, TTV, and RV methods.
L001246	None of these three methods are strongly biased towards or away from moderate eccentric exoplanets.
L001247	However, exoplanet systems with orbital eccentricities derived solely from TTV methods are biased towards resonant (or near-resonant) systems.
L001248	These TTV systems might have a different eccentricity distribution compared to other exoplanets in the comparison NEA sample.
L001249	To test for this effect, we remove all TTV systems (13 exoplanets in total, Fig.~\ref{fs18}A) in our comparison NEA sample and re-perform the fitting procedures.

L001253	\begin{equation}
L001254	\label{es27}
L001255	{\delta = \frac{P_{\rm out}}{P_{\rm in}} \frac{q-1}{q}-1},
L001256	\end{equation}

L001258	We also re-performed the fitting procedures after removing MMR systems.

L001276	\subsubsection*{\hypertarget{s8.2}{Effect of using single-transit systems}}
L001277	\noindent The fiducial Kepler single-transit exoplanet sample are more homogeneous than the comparison NEA samples.
L001278	Compared to the NEA samples, which consist of exoplanets with orbital eccentricities measured by RV and TTV methods, our Kepler samples rely on the TDR method to uniformly derive the mean eccentricities of exoplanets in each bin.
L001279	However, using the $P$--$e$ relation of single-transit exoplanet systems to represent the entire population might introduce biases.
L001280	To investigate this, we perform a forward modeling test.
L001281	
L001282	We generate one million simulated exoplanet systems assuming eccentricities are independent of orbital periods.
L001283	Specifically, we assign $R_\star$, $M_\star$, $N_{\rm p}$, $\omega$, $e$, $i$, $a$ and $P$ to each generated systems, where $N_{\rm p}$ is the number of exoplanets.
L001284	The radii and masses of the host stars are fixed to the solar values ($R_\star=1~R_\odot$ and $M_\star=1~M_\odot$).
L001285	$N_{\rm p}$ of each system is drawn from a Poisson distribution with a mean value of $\bar{n} = 3$\cite{2018ApJ...860..101Z,2020AJ....159..164Y}.
L001286	$\omega$ is drawn from a uniform distribution between 0 and $2\pi$.
L001287	$e$ is drawn from a uniform distribution  between 0 and 0.4.
L001288	Following previous work \cite{2016PNAS..11311431X}, we set the orbital inclinations of exoplanets (relative to the system invariant plane) to be equal to their eccentricities ($i=e$).
L001289	For $a$ and $P$ of exoplanets, we apply previous method\cite{2012AJ....143...94T,2018ApJ...860..101Z} to randomly draw $\xi\equiv R_\star/a$ according to the PDF:
L001290	\begin{equation}
L001291	\label{es28}
L001292	{\rm PDF(\xi)} = \frac{0.36}{\xi}\frac{\left(\frac{\xi}{0.074}\right)^{0.04}}{1+\left(\frac{\xi}{0.074}\right)^{3.18}},
L001293	\end{equation}
L001294	for $0.004<\xi<0.6$.
L001295	This PDF accounts for the correction of geometric transit probability\cite{2012AJ....143...94T,2018ApJ...860..101Z}.
L001296	We then obtain $a$ and $P$ from $\xi$.
L001297	\end{multicols}

L001316	\begin{multicols}{2}
L001317	After the generation, we conduct a simple simulation of transit observation to the generated exoplanet systems to acquire single-transit and multi-transit exoplanet samples.
L001318	Specifically, we calculate $b$ of each generated exoplanet to determine whether it would be observed.
L001319	Assuming the distribution of $I$ (inclination of the system invariable plane relative to the observer) is isotropic (${\rm cos}I$ follows a uniform distribution between -1 and 1), the exoplanet inclination relative to the observer $I_{\rm p}$ is given by\cite{2018ApJ...860..101Z}:
L001320	\begin{equation}
L001321	\label{es29}
L001322	I_{\rm p} = {\rm arccos}({\rm cos}I\,{\rm cos}i-{\rm sin}I\,{\rm sin}i\,{\rm cos}\phi),
L001323	\end{equation}
L001324	where $\phi$ is the longitude of ascending node of the exoplanet (also termed the phase angle, which represents the orientation of the orbital plane of the exoplanet), which we randomly drew from a uniform distribution between 0 and $2\pi$.
L001325	Combining Eq.~\ref{es29} with Eq.~\ref{es3}, we obtain $b$ for each generated system, and the exoplanets with $|b|<=1$ are considered potentially observable.
L001326	We then record the orbital periods and eccentricities of these exoplanets, and categorize their systems as single-transit or multi-transit.
L001327	The $P$--$e$ distribution of all the observable simulated systems is shown in Fig.~\ref{fs19}A, single-transit exoplanets (singles) in Fig.~\ref{fs19}B and multiple-transit exoplanets (multiples) in Fig.~\ref{fs19}C.
L001328	We find singles tend to have higher eccentricities, while multiples tend to have lower eccentricities, consistent with previous work\cite{2015ApJ...808..126V,2016PNAS..11311431X,2019AJ....157...61V}.
L001329	To investigate the $P$--$e$ relations of singles and multiples, we divide these systems into nine bins according to their orbital periods (similar to our fiducial Kepler sample).
L001330	We calculate the mean orbital periods and mean eccentricities in each bin, and fitted a power-law model same as our fiducial Kepler sample to their $\bar{P}$--$\bar{e}$ distributions.
L001331	Fig.~\ref{fs19}D-F show that the $\bar{P}$--$\bar{e}$ relation of our simulated transits resembles the input intrinsic relation (with $k=0.2$ and $c=0$).
L001332	However, the singles tend to show a positive $\bar{P}$--$\bar{e}$ correlation and the multiples tend to show an anti-correlation between $\bar{P}$ and $\bar{e}$.
L001333	This is because lower orbital inclinations (eccentricities) are required for exoplanets with longer periods in multiple-transit systems to be observable.
L001334	
L001335	The $\bar{P}$--$\bar{e}$ relations induced by this observational bias are at least an order of magnitude smaller than what our observed ones.
L001336	The increase/decrease of orbital eccentricities from 1 to 100 days is $\sim 0.02$, which is ten times smaller than we observed.
L001337	Therefore, the variation in the power-law index $c$ induced by the observational bias is negligible compared to the $1~\sigma$ uncertainties in our results for both SEs and MNs.

L001339	\subsection*{\hypertarget{s9}{Effect of stellar metallicity}}
L001340	\noindent For small exoplanets, there is an anti-correlation between orbital period and stellar metallicity\cite{2013A&A...560A..51A,2016AJ....152..187M}, and a positive correlation between stellar metallicity and orbital eccentricity\cite{2019AJ....157..198M,2023AJ....165..125A}.
L001341	The combination of these two relations could induce an anti-correlation between orbital period and eccentricity.
L001342	To investigate this effect, we utilize the Kepler-LAMOST small single-transit planet sample from previous work\cite{2023AJ....165..125A}.
L001343	This sample contain precise and homogeneous stellar metallicity measurements from LAMOST data release 8\cite{2012RAA....12.1197C} for small single-transit Kepler planets with $R<4R_\oplus$.
L001344	We obtain a period--metallicity relation from this sample:
L001345	\begin{equation}
L001346	\label{es30}
L001347	{\rm [Fe/H]} = -0.028~{\rm log}_{10}\left(\frac{P}{10\;{\rm days}}\right)-0.020, \\
L001348	\end{equation}
L001349	where [Fe/H] is stellar metallicity.
L001350	Eq.~\ref{es30} shows an anti-correlations between stellar metallicities and orbital periods, consistent with previous works\cite{2013A&A...560A..51A,2016AJ....152..187M}.
L001351	Because the orbital eccentricities of small exoplanets are positively correlated with the metallicities of their host star\cite{2019AJ....157..198M,2023AJ....165..125A}, this anti-correlation between planetary orbital period and stellar metallicity will induce a $P$--$e$ anti-correlations.
L001352	This projected $P$--$e$ anti-correlation could potentially weaken the observed positive $P$--$e$ correlation of SEs and strengthen the observed $P$--$e$ anti-correlation of MNs.
L001353	
L001354	To remove the influence of the stellar metallicities, we utilize the metallicity--eccentricity relation for single-transit small exoplanets found in previous work\cite{2023AJ....165..125A}: $\bar{e}\propto10^{1.78\cdot{\rm \overline{[Fe/H]}}}$ (which is derived using the same Kepler-LAMOST sample mentioned above).
L001355	Based on this metallicity--eccentricity relation, we calculate corrected mean eccentricities:
L001356	\begin{equation}
L001357	\label{es31}
L001358	\bar{e}' = \bar{e} \cdot 10^{-1.78\cdot{\rm \overline{[Fe/H]}}},
L001359	\end{equation}
L001360	where $\bar{e}$ and $\overline{\rm [Fe/H]}$ are the mean eccentricities (before correction) and mean metallicities (from Eq.~\ref{es30}) in each bin, respectively.
L001361	$\overline{\rm [Fe/H]}>0$ corresponds to $\bar{e}'<\bar{e}$, and vice versa.
L001362	
L001363	After correcting the effect of stellar metallicity, we perform the same fitting procedures as our fiducial Kepler sample to the $\bar{P}-\bar{e}'$ distributions of SEs and MNs (Fig.~\ref{fs20}.)
L001364	For SEs, the positive $P$--$e$ correlation after metallicity correction is stronger (a larger power-law index of $c=0.43$ and a lower p-value of $7.1\times13^{-3}$) than was measured for our fiducial Kepler sample.
L001365	For MNs, the $P$--$e$ anti-correlation after metallicity correction becomes weaker (a larger index of $c=-0.39$) than was measured for our fiducial Kepler sample, but the p-value $4.6\times13^{-3}$ remains small (corresponding to a significance level of $2.8~\sigma$).
L001366	For both SEs and MNs, the power-law indices $c$ after the metallicity correction are closer to the values of theoretical predictions (Fig.~\ref{fs20}C).
L001367	
L001368	We conclude that the combination of period--metallicity and metallicity--eccentricity relations can partially explain the observed $P$--$e$ anti-correlation for MNs, and potentially weakens the observed positive $P$--$e$ correlation of SEs.
L001369	After correcting for this effect, the positive $P$--$e$ relation of SEs strengthens, and the $P$--$e$ anti-correlation of MNs weakens.
L001370	Nevertheless, the $P$--$e$ relations remain different between SEs and MNs after the correction: the posterior probability distributions of $c$ for SEs and MNs (Fig.~\ref{fs20}C) overlap by a fraction of $2.9\times13^{-3}$, corresponding to a significance level of $\sim 3.6~\sigma$.
L001371	\end{multicols}

L001384	\begin{multicols}{2}
L001385	\subsection*{\hypertarget{s10}{Previous studies}}
L001386	\noindent Previous works have studied the eccentricity distribution of small exoplanets\cite{2015ApJ...808..126V,2019AJ....157...61V,2020A&A...635A..37C,2024AJ....168..115B}, however, none of them reported the relations between orbital periods and eccentricities that we found in this work.
L001387	Here we consider why our results differ from theirs
L001388	
L001389	Our samples have smaller eccentricity uncertainties compared to previous works.
L001390	Previous studies\cite{2015ApJ...808..126V,2019AJ....157...61V} investigated the orbital eccentricities of small Kepler exoplanets using the eccentricities of individual exoplanets, which have large uncertainties.
L001391	Our TDR method instead investigates the mean eccentricities of a group of exoplanets (in each bin), which reduces the uncertainties.
L001392	Fig.~\ref{fs21} shows our fiducial Kepler and comparison NEA samples have smaller uncertainties ($u \equiv 0.5\varepsilon + 0.05<0.1$).
L001393	Most of the exoplanets in previous studies have larger eccentricity uncertainties.
L001394	As discussed above, the $P$--$e$ relations we found would be obscured by the those higher uncertainties.
L001395	
L001396	Previous studies did not separate their samples into SEs and MNs: they either investigated the small exoplanets with $R<6~R_\oplus$\cite{2015ApJ...808..126V,2019AJ....157...61V}, small exoplanets with $R<3~R_\oplus$\cite{2020A&A...635A..37C}, or low-mass exoplanets with $m<0.165~M_{\rm J}$\cite{2024AJ....168..115B}.
L001397	Because we find that SEs and MNs follow opposite $P$--$e$ relations, mixing these two populations could produce a flat eccentricity-period distribution as they found.
L001398	\end{multicols}
